title: You Didn’t Wake Up Lukewarm. You Just Said “Tomorrow” to Jesus Too Many Times.
paragraphs: You Didn’t Wake Up Lukewarm. You Just Said “Tomorrow” to Jesus Too Many Times.
The frightening thing about spiritual drift is that it rarely feels like walking away from Jesus. Sometimes it just feels like telling Him, “Tomorrow.”
You probably never planned to become distant from God.
That may be the most unsettling part.
There probably wasn’t a morning when you opened your eyes, stared at the ceiling, and decided:
“I think I’ll become lukewarm today.”
You didn’t schedule spiritual numbness.
You didn’t write “neglect Jesus” into your calendar.
You didn’t necessarily stop believing the Gospel.
You didn’t wake up wanting a hardened heart.
It happened more quietly than that.
You were tired.
Busy.
Distracted.
Hurting.
Disappointed.
Maybe angry.
Maybe ashamed.
Maybe life simply became so loud that the voice you once listened for became easier to postpone.
You meant to pray.
Tomorrow.
You felt the conviction to forgive somebody.
Later.
You knew that habit was beginning to own you.
Soon.
You sensed God pressing on something hidden that needed to be confessed.
Not tonight.
You wanted to return to Scripture.
When life calms down.
You knew you needed to obey.
After one more compromise.
And somehow...
tomorrow kept becoming today.
Then today kept becoming another tomorrow.
Until one day, something that once would have broken your heart barely bothered you anymore.
That is what makes spiritual drift terrifying.
It does not always begin with hatred for Jesus.
Sometimes it begins with postponement.
And Hebrews gives us a warning that is far more personal than many of us realize:

“Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God. But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.”
— Hebrews 3:12–13, KJV
Read that last phrase again.
“...hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.”
The Greek is striking.
The word translated “hardened” is σκληρυνθῇ — sklērynthē, from σκληρύνω — sklērynō, meaning to become hard or to be hardened.
And the phrase translated “deceitfulness of sin” contains ἀπάτῃ τῆς ἁμαρτίας — apatē tēs hamartias.
The deception of sin.
The deceitfulness of sin.
Sin does not always walk through the front door announcing what it intends to destroy.
It deceives.
It minimizes.
It whispers.
Not, “Abandon Christ forever.”
Just...
“Not today.”
That is often enough.
Because tomorrow can become one of the most spiritually dangerous words in your vocabulary when Jesus is calling you to obey today.
Tomorrow I’ll pray.
Tomorrow I’ll confess.
Tomorrow I’ll forgive.
Tomorrow I’ll stop.
Tomorrow I’ll surrender this relationship.
Tomorrow I’ll deal with the bitterness.
Tomorrow I’ll open my Bible again.
Tomorrow I’ll come back.
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
And somewhere between all those tomorrows, the heart can begin learning how to live comfortably with what once disturbed it.
That is why Hebrews says:
“...while it is called To day...”
The Greek word is σήμερον — sēmeron.
Today.
Not someday.
Not when your emotions cooperate.
Not when temptation becomes easier.
Not when your schedule clears.
Not when you finally feel spiritual again.
Today.
There is an urgency in Hebrews because the human heart does not remain unaffected by repeated resistance.
Every time conviction is dismissed, resistance can become easier.
Every time obedience is postponed, postponement can begin feeling normal.
Every time sin is excused, the excuse can become more believable.
And eventually a person may still know Christian language...
still repost Christian content...
still say “God is good”...
still attend church...
still own a Bible...
still know worship songs...
and yet quietly become accustomed to living at a distance from the One whose name they confess.
That is what makes lukewarmness so frighteningly recognizable.
It does not always look like somebody shaking a fist at heaven.
Sometimes it looks like someone who still loves the idea of Jesus but keeps rescheduling surrender.
And maybe that sentence hurt.
Maybe because you recognize yourself in it.
There was a time when you prayed differently.
There was a time when Scripture could stop you in your tracks.
There was a time when conviction brought tears.
There was a time when you hated the thought of grieving God.
There was a time when worship was not background noise.
There was a time when you wanted Jesus more than you wanted comfort.
But something happened.
Maybe there wasn't even one dramatic scandal.
Maybe that is precisely the problem.
Nothing exploded.
Nothing looked catastrophic.
You just drifted.
A missed prayer became a prayerless week.
A prayerless week became normal.
One compromise became another.
One secret became a hiding place.
One excuse became a lifestyle.
One delayed act of obedience became another unfinished conversation with God.
And eventually you learned something dangerous:
how to postpone Jesus without feeling like you had rejected Him.
But Scripture never treats the condition of the heart casually.
Hebrews does not say, “Relax. You still have plenty of time.”
It says:
“Take heed...”
Watch yourself.
Pay attention.
Because hearts can harden.
Sin can deceive.
People can depart from the living God.
And we need one another urgently enough that Hebrews commands believers to encourage one another daily.
Daily.
Because Christianity was never meant to be a private arrangement between you and your preferences.
We need brothers and sisters who love us enough to interrupt our drift.
People who will remind us of Christ when our hearts become tired.
People who will not applaud what is destroying us.
People who will say, “Come back.”
Maybe this article is that interruption for somebody today.
Maybe for you.
And if you feel exposed right now, do not mistake conviction for rejection.
The Gospel is not the story of Jesus waiting for sufficiently clean people to approach Him.
The Gospel is the announcement that the Son of God came for sinners.
Jesus said:
“They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
— Luke 5:31–32, KJV
Do you see it?
The answer to spiritual drift is not pretending you never drifted.
It is returning to Christ.
The answer to sin is not better camouflage.
It is repentance.
The answer to shame is not hiding longer.
It is coming into the light and trusting the mercy purchased by Jesus Christ.
Because the same Bible that warns about hardened hearts also tells us:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— 1 John 1:9, KJV
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Those are Gospel words.
Your sin is serious.
But Christ is not a weak Savior.
Your drift matters.
But you are not being told to repair yourself sufficiently before approaching Him.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Confess what you have been protecting.
Put down what you have been excusing.
Open the Scriptures you have been avoiding.
Pray the prayer you keep postponing.
Forgive the person whose name makes your chest tighten.
Ask forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Not because these actions purchase salvation.
They cannot.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works.
But grace does not make sin precious.
Grace teaches us to leave it.
Jesus did not endure the cross so we could become comfortable in the chains He came to break.
At Calvary, sin was not treated as a minor inconvenience.
Christ bore our sins.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The righteous for the unrighteous, that He might bring us to God.
And then the grave did not get the final word.
Jesus rose.
That means your story does not have to end where your compromise left you.
Your worst chapter does not have authority over the Author.
Your secret does not outrank His mercy.
Your shame does not have more power than His blood.
Your wandering does not make repentance meaningless.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples fled.
Paul once persecuted the church of Christ.
Scripture is filled with human wreckage interrupted by divine mercy.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But notice what grace does not say.
Grace does not say:
“Keep sleeping.”
Grace says:
“Wake up.”
Grace does not whisper:
“Stay exactly where sin left you.”
Grace calls:
“Come.”
And maybe the word your soul needs most right now is the word Hebrews already gave you.
Today.
Today, pray.
Even if you feel nothing.
Today, confess.
Even if your pride screams.
Today, forgive.
Even if your emotions have not caught up.
Today, open your Bible.
Even if you only manage a few verses.
Today, turn away from what you know is pulling you from Christ.
Today, stop negotiating with the thing God has already convicted you about.
Today, tell another believer that you are struggling.
Today, come home.
Because nobody knows how many tomorrows they have.
And there is something else you need to hear.
Do not turn this article into another moment of conviction that disappears beneath your thumb.
If this exposed something hidden in you, be honest.
Not because typing words earns grace.
It doesn't.
But sometimes bringing what is hidden into the light begins with finally refusing to pretend.
And read the comments too.
Someone underneath this article may need to discover that they are not the only believer who has struggled.
Encourage them.
Pray for them.
Remind them of Christ.
Hebrews did not merely warn us against hardened hearts. It told us to exhort one another daily.
So do that.
And think of one person while you are reading this.
The friend who has slowly disappeared from church.
The son who says he still believes but wants nothing to do with God right now.
The daughter carrying shame nobody sees.
The husband silently drifting.
The wife spiritually exhausted.
The believer who still smiles on Sunday but has been losing the battle privately.
The skeptic who assumes Christianity has nothing to say to broken people.
The Christian whose faith has slowly become an accessory instead of a consuming allegiance to Christ.
Send this to them.
Let your timeline carry something eternal.
If the Gospel has given you life, use whatever reach God has placed in your hands to point people toward Jesus.
Sharing cannot save anyone.
Buying Christian products cannot save anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But believers can use their time, resources, voices, platforms, and generosity to help biblical truth travel farther.
Not to purchase God's favor.
Not to prove your Christianity.
Not because God needs your money.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him, and one expression of that surrender can be generously supporting faithful Gospel work when we are able.
And there is more available even without paying.
Not because every sentence is unforgettable.
And when it does, come back and remember Hebrews:
“...while it is called To day...”
And before you leave...
ask yourself the question you may have avoided through this entire article.
What have I been telling Jesus I will surrender tomorrow?
Name it.
Bring it into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Run toward Christ.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy would not be that you openly screamed “No” at Jesus.
Perhaps it would be that you whispered “tomorrow” so many times that eventually your heart stopped trembling when He called.
But if you can still hear Him...
if His Word is still cutting through the noise...
if conviction is disturbing your comfortable distance...
do not waste that moment.
Today.
Come back today.
Because the heart that keeps saying “tomorrow” may one day forget why it ever wanted Jesus today.
